1
夫龜文成象，肇八卦於庖犧； 鳥跡分形，創六書於蒼頡。 聖作明述，同源異流。 《墳》《典》起之於前，《詩》《書》繼之於後。 先王陳跡，後王準繩。 《易》曰：「觀乎人文以化成天下。」 《禮》曰：「君子如欲化民成俗，其必由學乎！」 學者非他，方策之謂也。 琢玉成器，觀古知今，歷代哲王，莫不崇尚。 自仲尼沒而微言絕，七十子喪而大義乖。 嬴氏坑焚，以愚黔首； 漢興學校，復創石渠。 雄、向校讎于前，馬、鄭討論於後，兩京載籍，由是粲然。 及漢末還都，焚溺過半。 爰自魏、晉，迄于周、隋，而好事之君，慕古之士，亦未嘗不以圖籍為意也。 然河北江南，未能混一； 偏方購輯，卷帙未弘。 而荀勖、李充、王儉、任昉、祖暅，皆達學多聞，曆世整比，群分類聚，遞相祖述。 或為七錄，或為四部，言其部類，多有所遺。 及隋氏建邦，寰區一統，煬皇好學，喜聚逸書，而隋世簡編，最為博洽。 及大業之季，喪失者多。 貞觀中，令狐德棻、魏徵相次為秘書監，上言以籍亡逸，請行購募，並奏引學士校定。 群書大備。
When the tortoise's markings formed images, Fu Xi first traced the Eight Trigrams; When bird tracks divided into shapes, Cang Jie created the Six Scripts. Sages created and the wise expounded — one source, many streams. The Canon and the Classic arose first; the Odes and the Documents followed after. Former kings left their traces; later kings took them as their measure. The Book of Changes says: "Observe the patterns of culture to transform the world." The Book of Rites says: "If a gentleman wishes to transform the people and establish custom, must he not begin with learning!" Learning is nothing other than what is called written records. Polish jade to make a vessel; observe antiquity to know the present — sage-kings of every age have none failed to honor this. After Confucius died, subtle words ceased; when the seventy disciples passed away, great principles diverged. The house of Qin buried and burned books to keep the common people ignorant; When Han rose, schools were restored and the Stone Canal established anew. Liu Xiang and Liu Xin collated texts in the earlier age; Ma Rong and Zheng Xuan debated them in the later — the libraries of the two capitals thereby blazed with brilliance. By the end of Han, when the capital returned westward, more than half were burned or drowned. From Wei and Jin down to Zhou and Sui, rulers who loved antiquity and scholars who admired the old likewise never failed to keep written records in mind. Yet north of the Yellow River and south of the Yangtze could not be unified; regional purchases and compilations left collections still incomplete. Yet Xun Xu, Li Chong, Wang Jian, Ren Fang, and Zu Geng were all broadly learned and well informed; generation after generation they arranged and compared, grouped and classified, each following the last. Some made Seven Records, others Four Divisions — yet in speaking of their categories, much was left out. When the house of Sui established its state and the realm was unified, Emperor Yang loved learning and delighted in gathering lost books; of Sui's catalogues, none was more comprehensive. By the end of the Daye reign, many were lost. In the Zhenguan era, Linghu Defen and Wei Zheng in succession served as Director of the Palace Library; they memorialized that because books were lost, purchases should be made, and they also submitted scholars to collate and fix them. The corpus of books was fully restored.
2
四部者，甲、乙、丙、丁之次也。
The Four Divisions are ranked Jia, Yi, Bing, and Ding.
3
甲部為經，其類十二：一日《易》，以紀陰陽變化。 二曰《書》，以紀帝王遺範。 三曰《詩》，以紀興衰誦歎。 四曰《禮》，以紀文物體制。 五曰《樂》，以紀聲容律度。 六曰《春秋》，以紀行事褒貶。 七曰《孝經》，以紀天經地義。 八曰《論語》，以紀先聖微言。 九曰圖緯，以紀六經讖候。 十曰經解，以紀六經讖候。 十一曰詁訓，以紀六經讖候。 十二曰小學，以紀字體聲韻。
The Jia division comprises the Classics, with twelve categories: first, the Changes, to record yin-yang transformations. Second, the Documents, to record the exemplary models of emperors and kings. Third, the Odes, to record rise and decline and songs of praise and lament. Fourth, the Rites, to record cultural objects and institutional forms. Fifth, Music, to record sound, appearance, pitch, and measure. Sixth, the Spring and Autumn, to record deeds and their praise or blame. Seventh, the Classic of Filial Piety, to record heaven's norm and earth's righteousness. Eighth, the Analects, to record the subtle words of the sage. Ninth, charts and weft-texts, to record the prognostications of the Six Classics. Tenth, commentaries on the classics, to record exegesis of the Six Classics. Eleventh, glosses and explanations, to record lexical and semantic study. Twelfth, minor learning, to record character forms and phonology.
4
乙部為史，其類十有三：一曰正史，以紀紀傳表志。 二曰古史，以紀編年系事。 三曰雜史，以紀異體雜紀。 四曰霸史，以紀偽朝國史。 五曰起居注，以紀人君言動。 六曰舊事，以紀朝廷政令。 七曰職官，以紀班序品秩。 八曰儀注，以紀吉凶行事。 九曰刑法，以紀律令格式。 十曰雜傳，以紀先聖人物。 十一曰地理，以紀山川郡國。 十二曰譜系，以紀世族繼序。 十三曰略錄，以紀史策條目。
The Yi division comprises Histories, with thirteen categories: first, standard histories, to record annals, biographies, tables, and treatises. Second, ancient histories, to record events by year. Third, miscellaneous histories, to record irregular and mixed accounts. Fourth, hegemonic histories, to record the state histories of illegitimate dynasties. Fifth, diaries of activity and repose, to record the words and deeds of rulers. Sixth, old precedents, to record court edicts and commands. Seventh, official posts, to record ranks and grades of office. Eighth, ritual protocols, to record auspicious and inauspicious proceedings. Ninth, penal law, to record statutes, commands, formats, and models. Tenth, miscellaneous biographies, to record sages and eminent persons. Eleventh, geography, to record mountains, rivers, commanderies, and states. Twelfth, genealogical registers, to record clans and succession. Thirteenth, brief catalogues, to record entries in historical compilations.
5
丙部為子，其類一十有四：一曰儒家，以紀仁義教化。 二曰道家，以紀清淨無為。 三曰法家，以紀刑法典制。 四曰名家，以紀循名責實。 五曰墨家，以紀強本節用。 六曰縱橫家，以紀辯說詭詐。 七曰雜家，以紀兼敘眾說。 八曰農家，以紀播植種藝。 九曰小說家，以紀芻辭輿誦。 十曰兵法，以紀權謀制度。 十一曰天文，以紀星辰象緯。 十二曰歷數，以紀推步氣朔。 十三曰五行，以紀卜筮占候。 十四曰醫方，以紀藥餌針灸。
The Bing division comprises Masters, with fourteen categories: first, Confucianists, to record benevolence, righteousness, and moral transformation. Second, Daoists, to record clarity, stillness, and non-action. Third, Legalists, to record penal law and institutional codes. Fourth, Logicians, to record aligning names with realities. Fifth, Mohists, to record strengthening the root and economizing expenditure. Sixth, Diplomatists, to record persuasion and stratagem. Seventh, Eclectics, to record combined treatment of many schools. Eighth, Agriculturalists, to record planting and cultivation. Ninth, fictionists, to record popular sayings and street lore. Tenth, military methods, to record strategy and institutions. Eleventh, astronomy, to record stars, celestial signs, and astrological patterns. Twelfth, calendrical calculation, to record computation of qi and new moons. Thirteenth, the Five Phases, to record divination and prognostication. Fourteenth, medicine, to record drugs, formulas, acupuncture, and moxibustion.
6
丁部為集，其類有三：一曰楚詞，以紀騷人怨刺。 二曰別集，以紀詞賦雜論。 三曰總集，以紀文章事類。
The Ding division comprises Collections, with three categories: first, Songs of Chu, to record the laments of poets. Second, individual collections, to record rhapsodies, fu, and miscellaneous essays. Third, general collections, to record writings by subject.
7
煚等撰集，依班固《藝文志》體例，諸書隨部皆有小序，發明其旨。 近史官撰《隋書經籍志》，其例亦然。 竊以紀錄簡編異題，卷部相沿，序述無出前修。 今之殺青，亦所不取，但紀部帙而已。 而煚等所序四部都錄以明新修之旨，今略載之：
Jiong and others compiled their collection following the form of Ban Gu's Bibliographic Treatise; each division's books had small prefaces expounding their purport. Recently the historiographers compiled the Bibliographic Treatise of the Book of Sui; the form is the same. I consider that because records and compilations differ in title and scrolls and divisions follow one another, prefaces and expositions add nothing beyond what earlier editors already wrote. In the present green-silk binding we likewise take none of that, but only record divisions and scroll-counts. Yet the general catalogue of the Four Divisions that Jiong and others prefaced, to clarify the intent of the new compilation, is here briefly set down:
8
竊以經墳浩廣，史圖紛博，尋覽者莫之能遍，司總者常苦其多，何暇重屋復床，更繁其說？ 若先王有闕典，上聖有遺事，邦政所急，儒訓是先，宜垂教以作程，當闡規而開典，則不遑啟處，何獲宴寧。 曩之所修，誠惟此義，然禮有未愜，追怨良深。 于時秘書省經書，實多亡闕，諸司墳籍，不暇討論。 此則事有未周，一也。 其後周覽人間，頗睹闕文，新集記貞觀之前，永徽已來不取； 近書采長安之上，神龍已來未錄。 此則理有未弘，二也。 書閱不遍，事復未周，或不詳名代，或未知部伍。 此則體有未通，三也。 書多闕目，空張第數，既無篇題，實乖標榜。 此則例有所虧，四也。 所用書序，咸取魏文貞； 所分書類，皆據《隋經籍志》。 理有未允，體有不通。 此則事實未安，五也。 昔馬談作《史記》，班彪作《漢書》，皆兩葉而僅成； 劉歆作《七略》，王儉作《七志》，逾二紀而方就。 孰有四萬卷目，二千部書，名目首尾，三年便令終竟，欲求精悉，不其難乎？ 所以常有遺恨，竊思追雪。 乃與類同契，積思潛心，審正舊疑，詳開新制。 永徽新集，神龍近書，則釋而附也。 未詳名氏，不知部伍，則論而補也。 空張之目，則檢獲便增。 未允之序，則詳宜別作。 紕繆鹹正，混雜必刊。 改舊傳之失者三百餘條，加新書之目者六千餘卷。 凡經錄十二家，五百七十五部，六千二百四十一卷。 史錄十三家，八百四十部，一萬七千九百四十六卷。 子錄十七家，七百五十三部，一萬五千六百三十七卷。 集錄三家，八百九十二部，一萬二千二十八卷。 凡四部之錄四十五家，都管三千六十部，五萬一千八百五十二卷，成《書錄》四十卷。 其外有釋氏經律論疏，道家經戒符籙，凡二千五百餘部，九千五百餘卷。 亦具翻譯名氏，序述指歸，又勒成目錄十卷，名曰《開元內外經錄》。 若夫先王秘傳，列代奧文，自古之粹籍錄符，絕域之神經怪牒，盡載於此二書矣。
I consider that the canon is vast and historical charts abundant; those who search cannot cover all, and those who oversee constantly suffer from their multitude — who has leisure to pile bed upon bed and further multiply explanations? If former kings left defective canons and supreme sages left unfinished affairs, and state policy urgently requires it while Confucian instruction comes first, then one ought to set teaching as a standard and open the canon by clarifying rules — there would be no leisure to sit at ease; how could one obtain repose? What was compiled before truly held only this meaning, yet the rites were not fully satisfactory, and regret runs deep. At the time the Palace Library's classics were in fact much lost or missing, and the archives of the various offices left no leisure for discussion. This was one matter not fully accomplished — the first point. Afterward, in touring the realm, missing texts were often seen; the new collection recorded what preceded the Zhenguan era, but nothing since Yonghui was taken; recent books were gathered only above the Chang'an period; nothing since Shenlong was entered. This was a second point where principle was not fully extended. Books were not fully reviewed, affairs again not fully covered; sometimes names and ages were unclear, sometimes placement in divisions was unknown. This was a third point where form was not fully penetrated. Many books lacked entries yet numbers of divisions were listed in vain; without chapter titles, the labels were truly awry. This was a fourth point where the standard was impaired. The prefaces used all drew on Wei the Pure Minister; the book categories all followed the Bibliographic Treatise of the Sui. Principle was not fully acceptable; form not fully penetrated. This was a fifth point where the facts were not settled. Formerly Sima Tan wrote the Records of the Historian and Ban Biao wrote the Book of Han — each barely finished in two generations; Liu Xin wrote the Seven Summaries and Wang Jian the Seven Registers — more than two reign-periods passed before they were done. Who, then, with forty thousand scroll-titles and two thousand book-divisions, from first entry to last, could finish in three years and still seek precision and completeness — is that not difficult? Hence regret has always remained; I privately think to make amends. Then, sharing purpose with my colleagues, I accumulated thought and applied my mind, examined and corrected old doubts, and opened new standards in detail. The Yonghui new collection and Shenlong recent books were then released and appended. Where names were unclear and division unknown, discussion supplied the gaps. Empty listed entries were then found and added upon inspection. Unacceptable prefaces were then detailed and separately composed. Errors were all corrected; confusion necessarily excised. More than three hundred errors in old transmissions were corrected, and more than six thousand scrolls of new book entries were added. In all, the Classics register: twelve categories, 575 titles, 6,241 scrolls. The Histories register: thirteen categories, 840 titles, 17,946 scrolls. The Masters register: seventeen categories, 753 titles, 15,637 scrolls. The Collections register: three categories, 892 titles, 12,028 scrolls. In all, the Four Divisions register 45 categories, altogether governing 3,060 titles and 51,852 scrolls, forming the Bibliographic Record in 40 scrolls. Beyond these were Buddhist sutras, vinaya, treatises, and commentaries, and Daoist scriptures, precepts, talismans, and registers — more than 2,500 titles and 9,500 scrolls in all. Translators' names were also fully given, prefaces and expositions set forth their purport, and a catalogue of ten scrolls was further compiled, titled Inner and Outer Scriptural Record of the Kaiyuan Era. As for secret transmissions of former kings and profound writings of successive ages — choice compilations and talismanic records since antiquity, divine scriptures and strange documents from distant lands — all are fully loaded in these two books.
9
夫經籍者，開物成務，垂教作程，聖哲之能事，帝王之達典。 而去聖已久，開鑿遂多，苟不剖判條源，甄明科部，則先賢遺事，有卒代而不聞，大國經書，遂終年而空泯。 使學者孤舟泳海，弱羽憑天，銜石填溟，倚杖追日，莫聞名目，豈詳家代？ 不亦勞乎！ 不亦弊乎！ 將使書千帙於掌眸，披萬函於年祀，覽錄而知旨，觀目而悉詞，經墳之精術盡探，賢哲之睿思鹹識，不見古人之面，而見古人之心，以傳後來，不其愈已！
Writings and records open things, accomplish tasks, hand down teaching, and establish standards — the able work of sages and the perfected canon of emperors. Yet the sages have long departed and excavations have grown many; if one does not divide sources by category and clarify divisions, then the legacy affairs of former worthies may pass a whole age unheard, and the classics of great states may vanish empty year after year. It would make scholars a lone boat swimming the sea, weak wings relying on the sky, carrying stones to fill the ocean, leaning on a staff to chase the sun — never hearing titles, how could they know authors and ages? Is that not exhausting! Is that not ruinous! It will let one hold a thousand bundles in the palm's glance and unfold ten thousand cases across the years; reading the catalogue one knows the purport, viewing entries one grasps the words — the refined arts of the canon fully explored, the keen thought of sages and worthies all understood: though one does not see the faces of the ancients, one sees their hearts — to transmit this to those who come after, is that not better still!
10
其序如此。
The preface is thus.
11
煚等《四部目》及《釋道目》，並有小序及注撰人姓氏，卷軸繁多，今並略之，但紀篇部，以表我朝文物之大。 其《釋道錄目》附本書，今亦不取，據開元以籍為之志。 天寶已後，名公各著文章，儒者多有撰述，或記禮法之沿革，或裁國史之繁略，皆張部類，其徒實繁。 臣以後出之書，在開元四部之外，不欲雜其本部，今據所聞，附撰人等傳。 其諸公文集，亦見本傳，此並不錄。 四部區分，詳之於下。
Jiong and others' Catalogue of the Four Divisions and Catalogue of Buddhist and Daoist Writings both had small prefaces and authors' surnames noted; scrolls were numerous — all are now omitted, recording only chapters and divisions to display the greatness of our dynasty's cultural achievements. The Buddhist and Daoist catalogue appended to this book is likewise not taken; we follow the Kaiyuan catalogue of writings for this treatise. After the Tianbao era, eminent men each composed writings and Confucian scholars often produced treatises — some recording changes in ritual and law, others trimming the fullness or brevity of national history — all expanding their divisions; their number is truly great. I hold that books appearing later, outside the Kaiyuan Four Divisions, should not be mixed into their original divisions; according to what is known, they are appended to the biographies of their compilers. The collected writings of various lords and ministers also appear in their own biographies; these are not recorded here. The Four Divisions are distinguished in detail below.
